Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: 'Being followed or tracked' is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one and with the rest of the profile, which centers on grief, guilt, and generalized somatic alarm rather than a pursuit/persecution context. It stands apart from the other trigger items and does not connect plausibly to the memory content provided.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy' is not well aligned with the rest of the formulation and item set. The profile otherwise emphasizes guilt, grief, misery, fragmented/numb recall, and bodily false alarms after a loved-one trauma. A 'going crazy' appraisal is possible, but here it appears weakly supported by the trigger and memory content and feels clinically out of step relative to the otherwise bereavement/guilt-focused presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, severe guilt, misery, and a sense that life has been destroyed can be coherent. However, the specific appraisal 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is notably more global and suicidal in tone than the rest of the selected profile, and it is not supported by corresponding threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content. With the provided five components, this item stands out as insufficiently anchored to the rest of the formulation-relevant material, making the node less internally coherent.

vignette:
Tane Faleolo is a 24-year-old Samoan-American pharmacist who presents for his initial assessment reporting a PCL-5 score of 58, describing the months since his younger brother Sione's death as a period in which his life has become almost unrecognisable to him.

Sione was twenty when he died. On the night in question, Tane had been working a late shift and came home to find his brother unconscious on the kitchen floor of the apartment they shared. The smell reached him before anything else - a thick, sour wave of alcohol that clung to the air and to Sione's clothes. Tane moved through what followed with a terrible mechanical efficiency: calling 911, performing CPR, speaking to the paramedics who arrived and who worked on Sione in the same kitchen where they had eaten breakfast that morning. Sione had mixed alcohol with a prescription medication he had not been prescribed. He did not survive. What Tane has never been able to fully assemble into a coherent sequence is everything between finding Sione and the moment the paramedics told him there was nothing more to do - he can retrieve fragments, images, the texture of the linoleum under his knees, but he cannot narrate it to himself from start to finish, as though the event exists only as shards rather than a story.

In the weeks that followed, Tane attended the funeral with his family, and something about standing at the graveside - the formal grief of it, the flowers and the dark clothing and the sound of his mother's crying - lodted itself in him in a way he did not anticipate. He has not attended a funeral since, and when a colleague mentioned a family bereavement in passing, Tane found himself leaving the break room abruptly, offering no explanation. He drives a longer route to work to avoid passing the cemetery on Meridian Avenue.

The smell of alcohol is perhaps the most pervasive difficulty he encounters. Tane works in a retail pharmacy adjacent to a supermarket, and the liquor aisle is visible from the dispensary window. On several occasions he has had to ask a technician to cover the counter when customers arrive carrying shopping bags containing wine or beer. He has not told his supervisor why. He had come to believe that explaining himself would require telling the whole story, and he was not willing to do that - not because he was protecting himself, he thought, but because he was not sure the story existed in a form he could tell.

He has also become acutely attuned to people behaving badly in any register - a customer arguing with the pharmacy tech, a driver cutting someone off in the car park, a stranger speaking harshly on a phone call nearby. In these moments his body moves before he has formed a thought: his chest tightens, his hands go cold, and he is already scanning the room for something he cannot name. He is certain, in those seconds, that something is about to go very wrong, even when the moment passes without incident. His body, he told the intake clinician, seems to have decided that the world is permanently on the verge of catastrophe, and he cannot talk it out of that conclusion.

When he does allow himself to remember that night - and sometimes the memory arrives without his permission - he is flooded with guilt so intense it is almost physical. He finds himself returning, again and again, to the fact that he is a pharmacist, that medication safety is the substance of his professional life, and that he was not there. At other times the memory comes back emptied of feeling entirely, as though it happened to someone he read about once and barely remembers.

Tane describes himself as someone who used to find genuine pleasure in his work, in his family, in the future he was building. He was certain that person was gone. Nothing he does now - not work, not the occasional dinner with friends he has not yet stopped accepting invitations to - carries any sense of weight or purpose. What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his mother, who told him quietly that she was frightened for him. What he is most afraid of, he said at the end of the intake, is that she is right.
